paragraphs: Caution signals | This page corresponds to O*NET-SOC 33-3021.06, Intelligence Analysts. The official scope is to collect, analyze, or evaluate information from multiple sources such as law enforcement databases, surveillance, intelligence networks, or geographic information systems, and use intelligence to anticipate and prevent organized criminal activity such as terrorism. The core deliverable is a reviewable intelligence judgment with traceable grounds, rather than merely a conclusion. Risks include information without cross-checking, unclear source and timeliness labels, presenting inferences as facts, and unauthorized external disclosure or action recommendations. U.S. wages are not fixed as static figures (a current O*NET query entry point is provided). O*NET presents employment and outlook under the broader parent category Detectives and Criminal Investigators (a broader-category proxy): approximately 117,900 employed in 2024 and 117,100 in 2034, -1% growth for 2024—2034, and 7,800 projected openings. These are not projections for this precise occupation. Exact occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible evidence gap. If information uncertainty, deadline pressure, and confidentiality constraints are difficult for you to tolerate, treat them as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Taking responsibility for judgments | Fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same assignment: conduct sound intelligence analysis (define questions and intelligence needs, collect and connect information from multiple sources, cross-check and identify gaps, form reviewable inferences and reports, and produce traceable analytical records); manage standards and confidentiality (follow organizational and regulatory requirements for source and timeliness labels, boundaries for public and restricted information, authorization levels for external disclosure and action recommendations, and personal and case information handling); and accept clearly defined job responsibilities (take responsibility for your analysis and grounds, and seek guidance or refer action recommendations, external sharing, or disclosure through the required process). Test this through a verifiable exercise, such as preparing an intelligence assessment and evidence chain using entirely fictional public materials, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

To assess whether intelligence analysis suits you, first conduct a verifiable exercise using public or simulated materials: create an entirely fictional case or threat assessment scenario, and outline the process from defining the intelligence question, listing available sources and search parameters, collecting and connecting information, cross-checking and labeling timeliness, and identifying gaps and alternative hypotheses to forming judgments and recommendations. Mark checks and possible problems at each step (information without cross-checking, unclear sources and timeliness, inferences presented as facts, unlabeled gaps, and unauthorized external disclosure or action recommendations). Afterwards, check whether sources, timeliness, verification, and gaps are indispensable; action recommendations or external sharing beyond authority are referred or submitted for guidance; and the process leaves reviewable records. All materials must be entirely fictional public examples; do not use real case details, people involved in cases, or restricted information.

Fit signals | Work activities in O*NET 33-3021.06 primarily involve communicating with supervisors and colleagues, using computers, obtaining information, analyzing data, processing information, and establishing and maintaining relationships. If you are willing to continually investigate sources and evidence, separate hypotheses from conclusions and record them accurately, and work steadily within confidentiality and authorization constraints, these daily requirements may align with your working style. Interest and personality tools are only for designing trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Intelligence analysts correspond to O*NET-SOC 33-3021.06, Intelligence Analysts. The official scope is to collect, analyze, or evaluate information from multiple sources such as law enforcement databases, surveillance, intelligence networks, or geographic information systems, and use intelligence to anticipate and prevent organized criminal activity such as terrorism. A typical complete workflow is to define the intelligence question, collect and connect information, cross-check and identify gaps, form reviewable judgments and reports, and share or recommend within authorization. Current U.S. national wages for Detectives and Criminal Investigators (a broader parent-category proxy, not precise intelligence analyst statistics): a 2025 median of $93,790 per year; employment of 120,500 in 2025, little or no change for 2025—2035 (a grouped label), and 7,800 average annual openings (an overall projection, not attributed to AI). The exact occupational wage gap for China remains; industry averages are broad references only.

entries: Objects of work | Analyze intelligence within authorization and confidentiality boundaries, working with intelligence questions and needs, information and data from multiple sources, case and threat leads, and search and analysis tools.

Checkable outputs | Reviewable analytical records and evidence chains, source and timeliness labels, lists of gaps and alternative hypotheses, assessment reports and charts, and sharing or disclosure records. Results must be traceable to sources and search parameters.

Complete workflow | Define intelligence questions and needs → collect and connect information from multiple sources → cross-check and label timeliness → identify gaps and alternative hypotheses → form reviewable judgments and reports → share or recommend within authorization.

paragraphs: Key judgments | O*NET work context data show: email daily, 100%; indoors in a controlled environment daily, 87%; telephone conversations daily, 78%; face-to-face discussions daily, 70%; working with others extremely important, 64%; and exactness or accuracy extremely important, 57%. Judgments rely on source reliability and timeliness, the extent of cross-checking, and authorization and confidentiality requirements for sharing and disclosure.

Environment and pace | Work primarily involves desk analysis and communication: sitting continually or almost continually, 65%; constant contact with others, 52%; some freedom to schedule tasks, 70%; some freedom to make decisions, 52%; a 40-hour workweek, 74%; time pressure more than once a week, 48%; and moderate competition, 48%. Case milestones and intelligence needs drive the pace.

Research inputs | O*NET 33-3021.06 provides the precise occupational identity, tasks, work activities, and work context. The interest code is ICE (Investigative—Conventional—Enterprising), and the occupation is in Job Zone Four (65% report a bachelor's degree, 13% a master's degree, and 9% an associate or other two-year degree). It is not marked Bright Outlook; the main industry is government. Current U.S. national wages for Detectives and Criminal Investigators (a broader parent-category proxy, not precise intelligence analyst statistics): a 2025 median of $93,790 per year; employment of 120,500 in 2025, little or no change for 2025—2035 (a grouped label), and 7,800 average annual openings (an overall projection, not attributed to AI). The exact occupational wage gap for China remains; industry averages are broad references only.

The first checks concern the objects (intelligence questions and needs, information and data from multiple sources), inputs (source reliability and timeliness, search parameters, and sharing and disclosure authorization), and deliverables (analytical records and evidence chains, gaps and alternative hypotheses, and assessment reports and charts). Anything unverified must remain pending verification; intuition based on experience or proxy categories cannot replace sources and verification.

Assess the complete workflow in four steps: check inputs (confirm sources, timeliness, and authorization boundaries) → define the task (analyze only within authorization and confidentiality scope) → execute and document (complete cross-checking, gap labels, and audit trails to standard) → review and escalate (stop immediately and report unreliable sources, major gaps, or disclosure or action recommendations beyond authority). A complete workflow requires verifiable sources, verification, and authorization, rather than merely reaching a conclusion.

Boundaries with neighboring roles | This page covers only the precise occupation O*NET-SOC 33-3021.06, Intelligence Analysts. Neighboring occupations such as security managers, management analysts, security management specialists, financial risk specialists, and fraud examiners, investigators, and analysts differ in their objects of work, authorized scope, and responsibilities. They cannot be interchanged based solely on titles, and proxy categories cannot replace organizational authorization, licensing, or ultimate responsibility.

Security management | Core outputs are security governance, budgets, and risk acceptance. This occupation focuses on intelligence judgments and grounds; authorization levels and responsibilities differ, and shared risk terminology does not imply identical responsibilities.

Management analysis | Core outputs are analysis of organizational problems and recommendations for improvement. This occupation focuses on collecting and verifying intelligence from multiple sources; information sources and confidentiality boundaries differ, so roles cannot be interchanged based only on titles.

Security management specialist work | Core outputs emphasize security policies, controls, and compliance coordination. This occupation places greater emphasis on intelligence sources, cross-checking, and gap labels; evidence types and authorization boundaries differ and must be checked separately.

Financial risk specialization | Core outputs are financial risk identification and quantitative assessment. This occupation focuses on case and threat intelligence; data characteristics, methods, and disclosure requirements differ and cannot be applied interchangeably.
The objects of intelligence analysis work and AI boundaries: which steps may be assisted and which judgments people must remain responsible for.

Direct answer | AI can assist with multi-source information search and deduplication, classification of text and communication records, initial pattern and anomaly screening, and drafting charts and reports. People remain responsible within their authorization for defining intelligence questions, judging source reliability, cross-checking conclusions, gaps and alternative hypotheses, external sharing, and action recommendations. Task exposure does not mean job replacement or widespread adoption; formal use requires authorization, human review, and an audit trail. This page provides no replacement probability or timetable.

Use of evidence | O*NET 33-3021.06 supports task context; possible AI assistance and human control points are editorial analysis on this page. Overall employment projections cover 2025—2035 and are not attributed to AI; they do not supply adoption rates, replacement rates, or effects.

Differences in impact | Different steps within the same occupation may be affected differently. Steps more readily represented in text and checked afterwards (search and deduplication, classification, initial screening, and drafts) are candidates for tool trials; actual efficiency must be tested using samples from the role. Steps involving source reliability, cross-checking, gap judgments, and sharing and disclosure authorization require greater human responsibility.

Responsibility chain | From confirming intelligence questions and authorization through tool processing, human review, approval of judgments and sharing, and recordkeeping, every step must have a clear responsible person and traceable evidence. Intelligence judgments and action recommendations must not rely solely on a model.

Turning point | Editorial judgment: tools may help improve search and initial screening, but do not change who is responsible for source reliability judgments, cross-checking, gap identification, or disclosure authorization. A practical approach is to build strong source verification and evidence chain skills first, then introduce tools into low-risk steps that can be reviewed and traced.

Possible assistance: multi-source search and deduplication, classification of text and communication records, initial pattern and anomaly screening, and chart and report drafts. These outputs can be checked afterwards, but original sources and timeliness must still be revisited.

Human control points: revisit original sources and records, review key judgments, and take responsibility for source reliability, cross-checking conclusions, gaps and alternative hypotheses, sharing, and action recommendations.

Caution conditions | Risk signals include drawing conclusions without cross-checking, unclear source and timeliness labels, presenting inferences as facts, unlabeled gaps, and unauthorized external disclosure or action recommendations. Conclusion | Activity preferences align more closely with a combination of investigative inquiry, following procedures, and a business perspective (O*NET interest code ICE). However, interest codes can only help design trials; they cannot determine hiring eligibility or performance.

Conclusion | This page provides no validation evidence that personality tests predict performance in this occupation. Continue checking against real tasks, responsibility boundaries, and reviewable deliverables rather than drawing conclusions from a single label.

Conclusion | RIASEC or personality frameworks can only help formulate questions; they cannot replace work samples, learning ability, qualifications, and actual performance evidence for this occupation. No tool conclusion constitutes a hiring, authorization, or appointment decision.

Source and verification risk | Trigger: a single information source, no cross-checking, or unclear timeliness. Consequences: possible incorrect judgments and misleading conclusions. Controls: cross-check multiple sources, label sources and timeliness, and document verification. Boundary: final judgments follow organizational procedures and authorization.

Risk of conflating inferences and facts | Trigger: presenting inferences, hypotheses, or model outputs as established facts. Consequences: possible misjudgments and misallocated responsibility. Controls: distinguish facts from inferences, state confidence and alternative hypotheses, and retain evidence chains. Boundary: conclusion grading and release follow the authorization chain.

Confidentiality and disclosure risk | Trigger: sharing or externally disclosing restricted information beyond authorization. Consequences: possible leaks, harm to cases, and compliance risks. Controls: share within authorization and the minimum necessary scope, retain sharing records, and handle sensitive information under medium and location requirements. Boundary: authorized personnel approve disclosure and sharing under regulations and organizational policies.

Personal and case information risk | Trigger: processing or sending information about people involved in cases and related individuals beyond authorization. Consequences: possible compliance risks and harm to rights and interests. Controls: handle information within the minimum necessary and authorized scope and retain processing records. Boundary: information protection follows regulations and organizational policies.

Common escalation rule | Whenever sources, verification, or authorization conditions are insufficient, first stop the relevant step and hand over the facts, impacts, and unresolved issues in reviewable records to an authorized responsible person. Do not override confidentiality requirements, professional opinions, or organizational authorization, or substitute model output for intelligence judgments and disclosure decisions.

How to become an intelligence analyst: preparation, training, and a path of responsibility. Begin with intelligence processes, source and verification methods, data analysis tools, and confidentiality and compliance awareness. Training or certificates do not automatically confer security clearance or disclosure authority.

Preparation information | O*NET education responses of 65% bachelor's degree, 13% master's degree, and 9% associate degree describe respondents' answers; Job Zone Four is not a uniform statutory entry requirement. First check the role's education, background checks, analysis tools, and supervision; separately confirm clearance, disclosure, and law enforcement action authority with the organization and jurisdiction. Courses or certificates do not confer these permissions.

Jurisdiction-specific requirements | For the United States, O*NET preparation information represents typical routes alongside job training. In mainland China, job entry, confidentiality, and personal information protection requirements are governed by relevant regulations and organizational policies and must be checked separately; they cannot be applied interchangeably.

Qualification boundaries | Courses, certificates, or training do not automatically confer security clearance, disclosure authority, or authority to recommend action. Education, certificates, background checks, hiring, organizational authorization, security clearance, and disclosure authority are distinct statuses; specific requirements depend on the role and applicable rules.

Responsibilities by stage | At entry and trial stages, search, organize, and make preliminary judgments under supervision and with limited permissions. At later stages, independently assess intelligence and prepare reports within authorization, taking responsibility for sources, verification, and conclusions.

Reviewable evidence | Demonstrate ability with entirely fictional public materials: define an intelligence question, specify sources and search parameters, complete cross-checking and gap lists, and produce assessment conclusions and an evidence chain. Do not use real case details, people involved in cases, or restricted information; state the basis and assumptions.

Next action | Complete a fictional intelligence assessment and evidence chain task package and review record. Ask an experienced person to challenge your source verification, gap labels, and authorization boundaries, then use the feedback to decide whether to invest further in this direction. Demonstrate ability through observable deliverables rather than course names.

Transfer paths | Multi-source search and linking, cross-checking and evidence chains, data analysis tools, and documentation and communication are possible transferable skills. Security management, consulting, financial risk, and fraud investigation respectively require governance, consulting methods, financial quantitative analysis, or investigation procedures and qualifications. Proximity confers no authority.

title.text: Evaluating Intelligence Analysis as a Career: Work, Entry, and Risk Boundaries

subject.name: Intelligence Analysts
subject.summary: Intelligence analysts collect, analyze, or evaluate information from multiple sources such as law enforcement databases, surveillance, intelligence networks, or geographic information systems, and use intelligence to anticipate and prevent organized criminal activity such as terrorism. Work includes defining intelligence questions, collecting and connecting information, cross-checking and identifying gaps, forming reviewable judgments and reports, and sharing or recommending within authorization. Under this page's evidence policy, U.S. wages are not fixed as static figures; a current O*NET query entry point is provided. O*NET presents employment and outlook under the broader parent category Detectives and Criminal Investigators (approximately 117,900 employed in 2024 and 117,100 in 2034, -1% growth for 2024—2034, and 7,800 projected openings), labeled throughout as not representing this precise occupation. Exact occupational wages for mainland China were not obtained and are recorded as a visible data gap.
